results.summary: This is a half adder implemented in Wokwi that takes two single-bit inputs and produces a sum and carry output. It is tested by toggling the inputs and observing the XOR and carry results. External LEDs are used to display the outputs. The documentation is minimal, consisting only of a title and brief testing note, so little else can be said about the design.

This design produces the numbers 1 through 3 and drives eight LED outputs. It is used by turning on a switch associated with a number and observing the LED display and output. No external hardware is required. The documentation is very thin, with only a one-line description and a brief testing note, so the internal logic cannot be determined.

This is a simple full adder that takes two single-bit inputs plus a carry-in and outputs a sum and carry-out. It is tested by checking the outputs against the expected A plus B result. LEDs were used as external hardware during testing. The documentation is brief and the design is a standard educational full adder.

This is a 7-bit priority arbiter that takes seven inputs and asserts at most one of seven outputs, prioritizing the lowest active input. An eighth output toggles with a clock and reset signal. It is tested by connecting outputs to a 7-segment display or LEDs and verifying correct arbitration as inputs change. External hardware includes input switches, a 7-segment LED display, and possibly a button to step the clock.

This project has no meaningful description of its function, with the documentation stating only that the author cannot explain what it does. It is intended to be tested by running random inputs, and the author plans to add an external LED. The design is essentially undocumented and its behavior cannot be determined from the provided text.

This is a full adder that takes two single-bit inputs and a carry-in and outputs a sum and carry-out across two pins. It is tested by toggling the inputs and verifying the sum and carry behavior for each combination. An LED display is used as external hardware. The documentation is brief but sufficient to describe a standard educational full adder.

This is a 4-bit adder that takes two 4-bit inputs and produces a 5-bit sum output. It is tested by setting the two numbers on a DIP switch and observing whether the output LEDs light up in a way consistent with addition. External hardware includes a DIP switch and a 7-segment display or LEDs. The documentation is brief but clearly describes a standard educational adder.

This design is a Manchester encoder that converts incoming serial data into Manchester-encoded serial data using a finite state machine. It requires an encoder clock at twice the frequency of the input data. It is tested by applying serial data at frequency f and the design clock at twice that frequency, then checking the encoded output. External hardware mentioned includes logic gates, D flip-flops, and clocks.

This project is titled hello and its one-line description mentions BCD, but the documentation consists only of placeholder template text. There is no explanation of how the design works, how to test it, or what external hardware it needs. The design cannot be described beyond the hint that it may involve binary-coded decimal. The documentation is effectively absent.
